families.title: Square leftovers
families.mathematics: A card n stands for an n by n square of counters. Taking away whole bundles of m until fewer than m are left leaves n² mod m. The leftover depends only on n mod m, because m-wide strips cut off the square are whole bundles; and x and m − x always leave the same. Two cards x < y match exactly when the L between their squares, re-formed as a (y − x) by (x + y) rectangle, is whole bundles. For an odd prime p that happens only when x + y = p (Euclid’s lemma), so p gives (p + 1)/2 leftovers counting 0 and every nonzero one hides two cards. Composite sizes break the pairing: with 8, cards 1, 3, 5 and 7 all leave 1; with 9, cards 0, 3 and 6 leave 0; with 15, cards 1, 4, 11 and 14 leave 1. One size from 2 to 12 never tells cards 0 to 15 apart, and of the 55 pairs of sizes only 10 and 11 do.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card in the bin for its leftover, then press That’s all.

puzzles.title: Square leftovers playground
puzzles.objective: Build a square, bundle it and see what is left over.
puzzles.instruction: Build a square, bundle it and see what is left over.
puzzles.controls: + and − change the square’s side and the bundle size. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Clear takes the bundles apart.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters.
A bundle takes away whole bundles of the chosen size.
puzzles.idea: Free play with squares and bundles, sides 0 to 15 and bundle sizes 2 to 15.
puzzles.prerequisites: None. A grown-up can set up a square from the worksheet or the puzzles.
hints: Try a 7 by 7 square with bundles of 7.
Make a 10 by 10 square with bundles of 7: choose a 10 by 7 strip and press Bundle.
Compare 3 by 3 and 10 by 10 with bundles of 7.

parent.notice: Choosing a strip as wide as a bundle takes away a whole row of bundles at once.
parent.prompt: Can a square bigger than 6 by 6 leave something new with bundles of 7?
parent.explanation: The playground has no goal and never counts as solved. It holds the worksheet’s Problem 5: with bundles of 7, a 10 by 10 square loses a 10 by 7 strip (ten bundles) and then a 3 by 7 strip (three bundles), leaving the 3 by 3 corner, so 10 leaves what 3 leaves. Every side leaves what its leftover with 7 leaves, so sides 0 to 6 show every leftover.
parent.extension: Which bundle sizes from 2 to 15 leave nothing over from a 10 by 10 square? (2, 4, 5 and 10, the factors of 100 up to 15.)
parent.connection: n² mod m depends only on n mod m: the square of (n − m) and the square of n differ by whole strips of m.

puzzles.provenance: Week 97 materials (counters in squares and bundles) and Problem 5 (“Can a bigger input give a new output?”), the strips of the guide’s 100 = 70 + 21 + 9 diagram.

puzzles.title: Bundles of 4
puzzles.objective: Put each card from 0 to 3 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 4.
puzzles.instruction: Put each card from 0 to 3 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 4.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to see its square. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Tap a bin to put the card in it, or drag the card onto a bin. Undo takes back a bundle or a card move.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card in the bin for its leftover, then press That’s all.
puzzles.idea: With bundles of 4, squares of 0 to 3 leave only 0 or 1: bins 2 and 3 stay empty.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count up to about 10 counters, and press Bundle until fewer than a bundle is left; the app does the taking away. No reading once a grown-up has read How to play. Saying why a bin stays empty is for older children with a grown-up.
hints: Tap card 3 and press Bundle until fewer than 4 counters are left.
3 by 3 is 9 counters: two bundles of 4 and 1 left over.
Cards 0 and 2 go in bin 0; cards 1 and 3 go in bin 1.

parent.notice: Bins 2 and 3 stay empty: no card leaves 2 or 3.
parent.prompt: Could any square at all leave 2 with bundles of 4?
parent.explanation: 0 × 0 = 0 and 2 × 2 = 4 leave 0; 1 × 1 = 1 and 3 × 3 = 9 = 4 + 4 + 1 leave 1. Bigger squares repeat these, because cutting 4-wide strips off a square leaves a smaller square with the same leftover. So squares leave only 0 or 1 with bundles of 4: an even side makes whole bundles, an odd one leaves 1.
parent.extension: With bundles of 3 and cards 1 to 5, which bin stays empty? (Bin 2: puzzle 2.)
parent.connection: The leftovers squares can leave are the quadratic residues. With 4 they are 0 and 1, which is why a sum of two squares never leaves 3 with bundles of 4.

puzzles.provenance: Week 97, page 1: the worked example (input 3, bundles of 4, 9 = 4 + 4 + 1) and its bundles-of-4 table for inputs 0 to 3.

puzzles.title: Bundles of 3
puzzles.objective: Put each card from 1 to 5 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 3.
puzzles.instruction: Put each card from 1 to 5 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 3.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to see its square. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Tap a bin to put the card in it, or drag the card onto a bin. Undo takes back a bundle or a card move.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card in the bin for its leftover, then press That’s all.
puzzles.idea: Bundles of 3 never leave 2: a side that is a multiple of 3 leaves 0, and every other side leaves 1.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count up to about 10 counters, and press Bundle until fewer than a bundle is left; the app does the taking away. No reading once a grown-up has read How to play. Saying why a bin stays empty is for older children with a grown-up.
hints: Bundle card 2 and card 4. How many counters are left each time?
4 by 4 is 16 counters: five bundles of 3 and 1 left over.
Card 3 goes in bin 0; cards 1, 2, 4 and 5 go in bin 1.

parent.prompt: Can a square leave 2 with bundles of 3?
parent.explanation: 1, 4, 16 and 25 leave 1, and 9 leaves 0. Cutting 3-wide strips off a square leaves the square of the side’s leftover, 0, 1 or 2, and 0, 1 and 4 leave 0, 1 and 1. So no square leaves 2 with bundles of 3. A 4 by 4 square shows the strips: a 4 by 3 strip is four whole bundles, then a 3 by 1 strip is one more, and the 1 by 1 corner is left.
parent.extension: With bundles of 4 and cards 1 to 5, which bins stay empty? (2 and 3.)
parent.connection: This is the K–1 route the review card added to Week 97: build squares 1 × 1 to 5 × 5, put each in groups of 3 and ask whether one can leave 2.

puzzles.provenance: Week 97 review card, fix 1: the K–1 route (squares 1 × 1 to 5 × 5 in groups of 3; “Can a square leave 2?”).

puzzles.title: Bundles of 5
puzzles.objective: Put each card from 0 to 4 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 5.
puzzles.instruction: Put each card from 0 to 4 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 5.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to see its square. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Tap a bin to put the card in it, or drag the card onto a bin. Undo takes back a bundle or a card move.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card in the bin for its leftover, then press That’s all.
puzzles.idea: Cards 1 and 4 match, and so do 2 and 3: a card and 5 minus it always leave the same.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count up to about 10 counters, and press Bundle until fewer than a bundle is left; the app does the taking away. No reading once a grown-up has read How to play. Saying why a bin stays empty is for older children with a grown-up.
hints: Bundle card 4: 16 counters.
16 is three bundles of 5 and 1 left over, the same as card 1.
Card 0 in bin 0, cards 1 and 4 in bin 1, cards 2 and 3 in bin 4.

parent.notice: Bins 2 and 3 stay empty, and the other cards pair up: 1 with 4, 2 with 3.
parent.prompt: Why do 2 and 3 leave the same?
parent.explanation: 4 leaves 4 and 9 = 5 + 4 leaves 4; 1 leaves 1 and 16 = 15 + 1 leaves 1. The 3 by 3 square is the 2 by 2 square with an L of 5 counters round it: one more bundle. From 1 by 1 to 4 by 4 the L has 15 counters and re-forms as a 3 by 5 rectangle, three bundles. The L between an x by x and a y by y square always re-forms as a (y − x) by (x + y) rectangle, so x and 5 − x match.
parent.extension: With bundles of 7, which cards pair up? (1 with 6, 2 with 5, 3 with 4.)
parent.connection: The quadratic residues mod 5 are 0, 1 and 4. (m − x)² = m² − 2mx + x², so x and m − x leave the same for every bundle size m.

puzzles.provenance: Week 97, Problem 1 (bundles of 5, inputs 0 to 4: which inputs share an output, and which outputs cannot occur).

puzzles.title: Secret card
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to see its square. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Tap the bin to put the card in it, or drag the card onto the bin; tap a card in the bin and then the row to take it out. Undo takes back a bundle or a card move.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card with the bin’s leftover in the bin, and no other card, then press That’s all.
puzzles.idea: With bundles of 7, leftover 2 hides two cards, 3 and 4, which add to 7.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count small leftovers and keep looking after the first answer. Grades 2–3 and up, or younger children with a grown-up reading.
hints: Bundle a few cards and look for 2 counters left over.
Cards 3 and 4 both leave 2.

parent.notice: A child who finds card 3 and presses That’s all is told there is another.
parent.prompt: If a friend says their square left 2, which cards could it be?
parent.explanation: 9 = 7 + 2 and 16 = 14 + 2. The other squares leave 0 (card 0 only), 1 (cards 1 and 6: 36 = 35 + 1) and 4 (cards 2 and 5: 25 = 21 + 4). With bundles of 7 every leftover but 0 hides exactly two cards, x and 7 − x.
parent.extension: Play the worksheet’s secret game: one player chooses a card and says only its leftover with bundles of 7, and the other names every card it could be.
parent.connection: Week 97 Problem 2: with a prime bundle size each nonzero leftover hides exactly two inputs.

puzzles.provenance: Week 97, Problem 2 (a secret input with bundles of 7), for leftover 2.

puzzles.title: Bundles of 7
puzzles.objective: Put each card from 0 to 6 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 7.
puzzles.instruction: Put each card from 0 to 6 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 7.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to see its square. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Tap a bin to put the card in it, or drag the card onto a bin. Undo takes back a bundle or a card move.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card in the bin for its leftover, then press That’s all.
puzzles.idea: With 7, every leftover except 0 holds two cards that add to 7, and three bins stay empty.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count up to about 10 counters, and press Bundle until fewer than a bundle is left; the app does the taking away. No reading once a grown-up has read How to play. Saying why a bin stays empty is for older children with a grown-up.
hints: Card 0 has no counters at all.
Cards 1 and 6 both leave 1: 36 = 35 + 1.
Bin 0: card 0. Bin 1: 1 and 6. Bin 2: 3 and 4. Bin 4: 2 and 5.

parent.notice: Bins 3, 5 and 6 stay empty; bins 1, 2 and 4 hold two cards each, and bin 0 holds card 0 alone.
parent.prompt: How many different leftovers are there, counting 0?
parent.explanation: 0 leaves 0; 1 and 36 leave 1; 4 and 25 leave 4; 9 and 16 leave 2. That is four leftovers, 0, 1, 2 and 4, which is (7 + 1)/2. Because 7 is prime the pairs x and 7 − x are the only matches (puzzle 10 says why).
parent.extension: With bundles of 11, how many leftovers? (Six: puzzle 10.)
parent.connection: The quadratic residues mod 7 are 0, 1, 2 and 4.

puzzles.provenance: Week 97, Problem 3 (bundles of 7) and Problem 2’s inventory.

puzzles.title: Bundles of 8
puzzles.objective: Put each card from 0 to 7 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 8.
puzzles.instruction: Put each card from 0 to 7 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 8.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to see its square. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Tap a bin to put the card in it, or drag the card onto a bin. Undo takes back a bundle or a card move.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card in the bin for its leftover, then press That’s all.
puzzles.idea: 8 is not prime, and four cards share leftover 1: 1, 3, 5 and 7.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count up to about 10 counters, and press Bundle until fewer than a bundle is left; the app does the taking away. No reading once a grown-up has read How to play. Saying why a bin stays empty is for older children with a grown-up.
hints: Bundle card 3: 9 counters.
Every odd card leaves 1.
Bin 0: 0 and 4. Bin 1: 1, 3, 5 and 7. Bin 4: 2 and 6.

parent.notice: Bin 1 holds four cards, more than any bin with 7.
parent.prompt: Why does 3 match 1 here, when 3 and 1 don’t add to 8?
parent.explanation: Every odd square leaves 1 with bundles of 8: 9 = 8 + 1, 25 = 24 + 1, 49 = 48 + 1. Even squares leave 0 (0 and 16) or 4 (4 and 36). So three leftovers occur: 0, 1 and 4. The pairs x and 8 − x still match (1 with 7, 3 with 5, 2 with 6), but now 1 matches 3 as well: the L between 1 by 1 and 3 by 3 re-forms as a 2 by 4 rectangle, one whole bundle, because 8 = 2 × 4.
parent.extension: With bundles of 9, which bin holds the most cards? (Bin 0: 0, 3 and 6.)
parent.connection: With a composite bundle size, (y − x)(y + x) can be whole bundles without either side being one.

puzzles.provenance: Week 97, Problem 3 (bundles of 8: output 1 hides four inputs).

puzzles.title: Bundles of 9
puzzles.objective: Put each card from 0 to 8 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 9.
puzzles.instruction: Put each card from 0 to 8 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 9.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to see its square. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Tap a bin to put the card in it, or drag the card onto a bin. Undo takes back a bundle or a card move.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card in the bin for its leftover, then press That’s all.
puzzles.idea: With 9, leftover 0 holds three cards, 0, 3 and 6; with a prime only card 0 makes whole bundles.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count up to about 10 counters, and press Bundle until fewer than a bundle is left; the app does the taking away. No reading once a grown-up has read How to play. Saying why a bin stays empty is for older children with a grown-up.
hints: Bundle card 6: 36 counters.
36 is exactly four bundles of 9.
Bin 0: 0, 3 and 6. Bin 1: 1 and 8. Bin 4: 2 and 7. Bin 7: 4 and 5.

parent.prompt: Why does 6 by 6 come out in whole bundles of 9?
parent.explanation: A 6 by 6 square cuts into four 3 by 3 squares, four bundles; 3 by 3 is one bundle. So 0, 3 and 6 leave 0; 1 and 8 leave 1; 2 and 7 leave 4; 4 and 5 leave 7. Four leftovers occur: 0, 1, 4 and 7.
parent.extension: With bundles of 15, find every card that leaves 1. (Puzzle 9.)
parent.connection: When the bundle size is a square, 9 = 3 × 3, every multiple of 3 squares to whole bundles.

puzzles.provenance: Week 97, Problem 3 (bundles of 9: output 0 hides three inputs).

puzzles.title: One size
puzzles.objective: Choose a bundle size that gives cards 0 to 5 different leftovers.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Choose a bundle size that gives cards 0 to 5 different leftovers.
puzzles.instruction: Choose a bundle size that gives cards 0 to 5 different leftovers.
puzzles.controls: Tap bundle sizes to choose them, then press Try. The dots show the tries left; when they run out, Again starts over. Undo takes back a size; tries stay tried.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Choose bundle sizes so that no two cards leave the same, then press Try. A Try that fails shows two cards that still match.
Press Can’t if no choice can work.
puzzles.idea: A size makes a card and the size minus it match, so it must be at least 10, and 12 makes 2 and 4 match: 10 and 11 work.
puzzles.prerequisites: Compare a few small numbers and learn from a failed try. Grades 3–5; knowing that cards adding to the size match (from the sorting puzzles) helps.
hints: Try a size and look at the two cards that match.
Size 7 makes 3 and 4 match: cards that add to the size always match.
Try a size bigger than 9.

parent.notice: A failed Try shows two cards that add up to the size, except with 12, which shows 2 and 4.
parent.prompt: Which sizes can you rule out without trying them?
parent.explanation: Any size m makes x and m − x match. Up to 9 two different cards from 0 to 5 add to m (0 and m up to 5, then 1 and 5, 2 and 5, 3 and 5, 4 and 5), so they match. 12 makes 2 and 4 match (16 = 12 + 4). 10 leaves 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5 and 11 leaves 0, 1, 4, 9, 5, 3: all different.
parent.extension: Add card 6. Does any size from 2 to 12 still work? (No: puzzle 11.)
parent.connection: Because x and m − x match, one size m can tell apart at most the cards 0 to m/2, about half as many cards as the size.

puzzles.provenance: New, after the review card’s App fit (“choose bundle sizes from 2 to 12 whose leftovers tell sides apart”), with cards 0 to 5 so that one size works.

puzzles.title: Bundles of 15
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to see its square. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Tap the bin to put the card in it, or drag the card onto the bin; tap a card in the bin and then the row to take it out. Undo takes back a bundle or a card move.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card with the bin’s leftover in the bin, and no other card, then press That’s all.
puzzles.idea: Four cards leave 1 with bundles of 15: 1, 4, 11 and 14. Because 15 = 3 × 5, card 4 matches card 1.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count small leftovers and keep looking after the first answer. Grades 2–3 and up, or younger children with a grown-up reading.
hints: Card 1 leaves 1. Which card is 15 minus 1?
Cards 1, 4, 11 and 14 leave 1.

parent.notice: A child who expects pairs may stop at 1 and 14; That’s all then says there is another.
parent.prompt: Could another leftover hide even more cards?
parent.explanation: 1 = 1, 16 = 15 + 1, 121 = 120 + 1 and 196 = 195 + 1. Card 4 matches card 1 because the L between 1 by 1 and 4 by 4 re-forms as a 3 by 5 rectangle, one whole bundle; 11 and 14 are 15 − 4 and 15 − 1. Leftover 4 also hides four cards (2, 7, 8 and 13), while leftover 0 hides only card 0, as at a prime.
parent.extension: Which leftovers occur with 15? (0, 1, 4, 6, 9 and 10: six.)
parent.connection: 15 = 3 × 5: a square leaves 1 exactly when its side leaves 1 or 2 with 3 and 1 or 4 with 5, giving 2 × 2 = 4 cards (the Chinese remainder theorem).

puzzles.provenance: Week 97, Problem 4 (output 1 with bundles of 15, inputs 0 to 14).

puzzles.title: Bundles of 11
puzzles.objective: Put each card from 0 to 10 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 11.
puzzles.instruction: Put each card from 0 to 10 in the bin for its leftover with bundles of 11.
puzzles.controls: Tap a card to see its square. Slide across counters to choose a rectangle, or tap counters one at a time, then press Bundle; with nothing chosen, Bundle takes the next bundle. Tap a bin to put the card in it, or drag the card onto a bin. Undo takes back a bundle or a card move.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Put every card in the bin for its leftover, then press That’s all.
puzzles.idea: Six leftovers, (11 + 1)/2: card 0 alone, and pairs that add to 11.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count up to about 10 counters, and press Bundle until fewer than a bundle is left; the app does the taking away. No reading once a grown-up has read How to play. Saying why a bin stays empty is for older children with a grown-up.
hints: Cards that add to 11 land in the same bin.
5 by 5 is 25 = 22 + 3, so cards 5 and 6 go in bin 3.
Bin 0: 0. Bin 1: 1 and 10. Bin 3: 5 and 6. Bin 4: 2 and 9. Bin 5: 4 and 7. Bin 9: 3 and 8.

parent.notice: Five bins stay empty, and the six others hold card 0 alone or two cards that add to 11.
parent.prompt: With 3, 5, 7 and 11, how many leftovers are there each time? Is there a rule?
parent.explanation: 3 gives 2 leftovers, 5 gives 3, 7 gives 4 and 11 gives 6: (p + 1)/2, counting 0. Two cards x < y match exactly when the L between their squares, a (y − x) by (x + y) rectangle, is whole bundles. 11 is prime, so a rectangle is whole bundles of 11 only when a side is a multiple of 11; here y − x is less than 11, so x + y = 11. Card 0 matches nothing, and the other ten cards pair up into five leftovers.
parent.extension: Does the rule work for 8, 9 or 15? (No: they give 3, 4 and 6 leftovers.)
parent.connection: Euclid’s lemma (Week 96): a prime that divides a product divides one of its factors. There are (p − 1)/2 nonzero quadratic residues mod an odd prime p.

puzzles.provenance: Week 97, Problem 6 (a rule for odd primes: bundle sizes 3, 5, 7 and 11), with the review card’s counters picture for the pairing (fix 2: the L re-formed as a rectangle).

puzzles.title: One more card
puzzles.objective: Choose a bundle size that gives cards 0 to 6 different leftovers.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Choose a bundle size that gives cards 0 to 6 different leftovers.
puzzles.instruction: Choose a bundle size that gives cards 0 to 6 different leftovers.
puzzles.controls: Tap bundle sizes to choose them, then press Try. The dots show the tries left; when they run out, Again starts over. Undo takes back a size; tries stay tried.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Choose bundle sizes so that no two cards leave the same, then press Try. A Try that fails shows two cards that still match.
Press Can’t if no choice can work.
puzzles.idea: No size from 2 to 12 gives cards 0 to 6 different leftovers: 11 makes 5 and 6 match and 12 makes 2 and 4 match.
puzzles.prerequisites: Compare a few small numbers and learn from a failed try. Grades 3–5; knowing that cards adding to the size match (from the sorting puzzles) helps.
hints: Size 11 worked for cards 0 to 5. Try it here.
Cards that add to the size match, so the size would have to be 12 or more.
Size 12 makes 2 and 4 match, so every size has a match.

parent.notice: After a right Can’t, every size shows two cards it makes match.
parent.prompt: How do you know no size works, without trying all eleven?
parent.explanation: A size m makes x and m − x match. For every m up to 11, two different cards from 0 to 6 add to m (0 and m up to 6, then 1 and 6, 2 and 6, 3 and 6, 4 and 6, 5 and 6), and 12 makes 2 and 4 match (16 = 12 + 4). So no size from 2 to 12 tells cards 0 to 6 apart. Can’t needs one try first, and it is refused while a size works.
parent.extension: What is the smallest size that tells cards 0 to 6 apart? (13.)
parent.connection: The review card notes that one size never tells cards 0 to 15 apart; this puzzle shows the same obstruction with seven cards.

puzzles.provenance: New, as a contrast with puzzle 8: one more card makes every size fail, the review card’s “one size never works” at a smaller scale.

puzzles.title: Two sizes
puzzles.objective: Choose two bundle sizes that give cards 0 to 15 different pairs of leftovers.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Choose two bundle sizes that give cards 0 to 15 different pairs of leftovers.
puzzles.instruction: Choose two bundle sizes that give cards 0 to 15 different pairs of leftovers.
puzzles.controls: Tap bundle sizes to choose them, then press Try. The dots show the tries left; when they run out, Again starts over. Undo takes back a size; tries stay tried.
rules: Card n is a square of n rows of n counters. Take away whole bundles until fewer than one bundle is left: the counters left over are its leftover.
Choose bundle sizes so that no two cards leave the same, then press Try. A Try that fails shows two cards that still match.
Press Can’t if no choice can work.
puzzles.idea: Of the 55 pairs of sizes from 2 to 12, only 10 and 11 give cards 0 to 15 different pairs of leftovers.
puzzles.prerequisites: Compare a few small numbers and learn from a failed try. Grades 3–5; knowing that cards adding to the size match (from the sorting puzzles) helps.
hints: Which sizes worked for cards 0 to 5?
Each size makes x and size − x match, so the other size has to tell those two apart.
Try 10 and 11.

parent.notice: Each failed Try shows two cards that both sizes still match.
parent.prompt: Why can’t one size do it?
parent.explanation: One size m makes x and m − x match, and for m up to 12 two different cards from 0 to 15 add to m, so one size never works. With 10 and 11, two cards x < y match under 11 only when x + y is 11 or 22 or y − x is 11, since 11 is prime. If x + y = 11 or y − x = 11, then x + y and y − x are odd, so the rectangle (y − x) by (x + y) has an odd number of counters and is not whole bundles of 10. If x + y = 22, whole bundles of 10 need y − x to be a multiple of 5 and even, so 10, and then y = 16, past 15. Checking all 55 pairs shows that no other pair works.
parent.extension: Add card 16. Do 10 and 11 still work? (No: 6 and 16 match under both, 36 and 256.)
parent.connection: Two sizes give each card a two-part code. By the Chinese remainder theorem, leftovers with 10 and 11 together are leftovers with 110, and 16 is the first card that matches an earlier one (6: 256 − 36 = 220 = 2 × 110).

puzzles.provenance: The review card’s App fit (“choose bundle sizes from 2 to 12 whose leftovers tell sides 0 to 15 apart … of the 55 pairs only 10 and 11 work”, card_checks.py), with a budget of four tries.
